description: File extensions the two module graphs compile into a module.
why: crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/compiler.rs resolves and compiles the client graph; packages/ruvyxa/runtime/compiler.mjs does the same for the server and prerender graph. Each keeps its own list because neither can import the other's, and a project is built by whichever graph owns that lane. An extension one accepts and the other refuses is a build that succeeds on the client and fails at prerender with RUV1806 naming a dependency the application never wrote.
note: Both hosts match case-insensitively: sources with an upper-case extension exist on case-insensitive filesystems, and rejecting them in one graph only would be the same divergence in a costume. `extensions` is the canonical lower-case spelling; `acceptedCasing` pins the folding.
parserDialectNote: Which dialect the parser is given, once an extension is known to be compilable. TypeScript settles this by extension and never by contents, because the two readings are mutually exclusive: in a `.ts` file `<T>(x)` is a generic parameter list and `<string>v` a type assertion, while the same bytes in a `.tsx` file open an element. The Rust graph used to switch JSX on whenever its scan saw something element-shaped, which made both of those ordinary TypeScript forms fail to parse with a diagnostic pointing at the author's code — while the Node graph, which reads the extension alone, compiled the same file. The `.js` family is the one case where the extension decides nothing, so the source is asked: JSX in a `.js` file is common in the ecosystem, and a comparison such as `a<b` parses correctly under JSX anyway, because an element can only begin where a value is expected.

parserDialect.source: export const f = <T>(x: T): T => x;
parserDialect.why: A generic arrow. Under JSX this is an unclosed `<T>` element and the module does not parse.

parserDialect.source:
const v: unknown = 'a';
export const s = <string>v;
parserDialect.why: An angle-bracket type assertion — legal in `.ts`, and an element in `.tsx`.

parserDialect.source: export const f = <T>(x: T): T => x;
parserDialect.why: Extensions fold with the ASCII rule, so an upper-case name off a case-insensitive filesystem gets the same dialect.

parserDialect.source: export const f = <T>(x: T): T => x;
parserDialect.why: `.mts` and `.cts` are TypeScript under a different module system, not a different dialect.

parserDialect.source:
const v: unknown = 'a';
export const s = <string>v;
parserDialect.why: The same rule from the CommonJS side.
The extension is the whole reason `.tsx` exists.
JSX in a `.js` file is common in the ecosystem and the Rust graph already accepted it. Refusing it in the Node graph compiled a package for the browser and then failed the same package at prerender.
The `.js` family is decided by the source, whichever module system it names.
A spaced comparison has nothing element-shaped in it.

Minified code writes comparisons this way, so the scan reads it as an element. Accepted deliberately: JSX can only begin where a value is expected, so the parser still reads this as a comparison. Pinned so the leniency is a decision rather than a surprise.
The question is asked of the mask, so an element inside a string is text.
